learningObjectives: Build a Requirements structure using Folders, RequirementSets, and layered Requirements.
Apply Basic Weighting to indicate the relative importance of a Requirement.
Apply Complex Weighting using Frequency Class and Damage Class, and explain how the exponential formula spreads Requirements apart.
Read the Contribution (%) and Relative Weight (%) columns to use Requirements as a risk dashboard.
Explain the difference in auto-update behavior for Requirements before and after Tosca 10.3.

elements.description: A criterion the system under test is expected to fulfil — functional (e.g. 'a customer can pay with a Visa card') or non-functional (e.g. system security). Requirements are gathered from workshops with stakeholders, or from existing specs/BA documents.

elements.title: Structural hierarchy, top to bottom
items: Folder — organizes the Requirements section, usually mirroring the system or process structure; can be nested.
RequirementSet — sits inside a Folder; groups Requirements representing one aspect of the application (frontend, backend, non-functional) or one process view (a sprint, a regression cycle).
Requirement — created inside a RequirementSet; can contain sub-Requirements, forming layers.
Leaf Requirement — the lowest level; should be modeled down to about the size of a use case or user story, not more granular than that.

elements.description: Start from the highest-level functionality (e.g. Customer, Products, Order Process) and expand downward into sub-Requirements. Keep the tree shallow, non-redundant, and easy to read — depth for its own sake makes the structure harder to navigate, not more precise.

elements.text: Requirement / Sub-Requirement is created via 'Create Object' in the Ribbon, 'Create Requirement' in the Mini-Toolbar, or the shortcut Ctrl+N, Ctrl+R. 'Create Requirement (after this)' (Ctrl+,) instead adds a sibling at the same level as the currently selected Requirement.

bulletPoints: Same structure order every time: Folder → RequirementSet → Requirement → (optional) sub-Requirements.
In Agile projects, RequirementSets can map to sprints, and Requirements can be named/numbered after user stories.

elements.description: Every Requirement defaults to a Weight of 1 (equal importance). Basic Weighting lets you assign any value from 0-10 per Requirement; Tricentis' recommended best practice is to keep it simple and use a 1-5 scale.

Collapse all sub-Requirements first and weight the highest level — this tells you which broad area to start testing in. Then expand each Requirement and weight its Leaf Requirements — this tells you exactly which specific item to focus on inside that area.

bulletPoints: 0-10 range, but stick to 1-5 in practice for readability.
Weight top level first, then drill down — not the other way around.

elements.description: A single linear scale often can't distinguish importance clearly enough (is this a 3 or a 4?). Complex Weighting instead asks two separate business questions per Requirement and lets Tosca calculate the Weight for you.

elements.title: The two input values
items: Frequency Class — 'How often is this functionality used?'
Damage Class — 'How much financial damage would we incur if this functionality failed?'

elements.description: Weight = 2^(Frequency Class) × 2^(Damage Class). Both inputs are entered on a 0-10 scale (best practice: 1-5), and Tosca calculates the resulting Weight automatically — though it can be overridden manually. Because the formula is exponential (base 2 by default, adjustable on the RequirementSet's Properties tab), Requirements spread out more distinctly than a simple additive or linear scale would allow, which makes prioritization decisions clearer.

elements.text: As with Basic Weighting, weight the highest-level Requirements first, then expand and weight the Leaf Requirements.

bulletPoints: Frequency Class × Damage Class, combined exponentially — not added together.
Both values are estimates for comparison purposes, not precise financial figures.

elements.description: Shows a Requirement's share of risk coverage across the whole RequirementSet. Values are multiplied by their parent's weight going up the tree, so Contribution (%) reflects how much this Requirement matters to the project as a whole — not just to its immediate siblings.
Shows a Requirement's weight compared only to its siblings on the same level. Relative Weight values for elements on the same level always sum to 100%.

Once weighted, Requirements link outward: TestSheets (TestCase Design) link to Requirements, TestCases link to Requirements, and ExecutionLists link to whole RequirementSets. The ExecutionState column then reflects executed-TestCase results weighted by risk — a risk-based coverage statement, usable as a management report.

bulletPoints: Contribution (%) = weighted against the whole set (parent-adjusted). Relative Weight (%) = weighted against siblings only, always sums to 100% per level.

elements.term: Auto-update behavior differs by Tosca version
elements.description: In Tosca 10.2 and earlier, Requirements recalculate automatically the instant a linked object changes. In Tosca 10.3 and later, auto-update is OFF by default — recalculating on every change can be slow in large repositories with many users and objects.
When a Requirement's data is stale, an exclamation mark appears next to the affected RequirementSet. Select it and press F6, or click 'Update Outdated Values' in the Ribbon, to recalculate.

elements.text: To switch auto-update back on in 10.3+: Project >> Settings >> Commander >> General >> Advanced >> 'AutoCalculateRequirements' = On. Worth enabling on smaller projects where recalculation cost isn't a concern.

📄 Exercises 01a-01f (Create a Basic Structure, Basic Weighting, Expand the Structure, Weighting with Frequency & Damage, Structure Sprint #1, Weighting Sprint #1) — Official Tricentis Academy course material, not redistributed here. Access it inside the official course.

bulletPoints: Pre-10.3: always live. 10.3+: manual by default (F6 / Update Outdated Values), toggleable via AutoCalculateRequirements.

examPitfalls.title: Treating Complex Weighting as additive
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming Weight = Frequency Class + Damage Class.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The formula is exponential: Weight = 2^(Frequency Class) × 2^(Damage Class). This is what gives Complex Weighting its wider, clearer spread compared to a linear scale.

examPitfalls.title: Mixing up Contribution (%) and Relative Weight (%)
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming both columns always sum to 100%, or that they measure the same thing.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Relative Weight (%) always sums to 100% among Requirements on the same level. Contribution (%) is parent-weighted and reflects a Requirement's share of the entire RequirementSet, so it does not sum to 100% at every level.

examPitfalls.title: Expecting real-time Requirement updates in Tosca 10.3+
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Making a change elsewhere in the project and expecting the Requirements dashboard to reflect it immediately, then reporting stale numbers.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Since Tosca 10.3, auto-update is OFF by default for performance reasons. Watch for the exclamation mark on the RequirementSet, and press F6 or 'Update Outdated Values' to refresh — or turn AutoCalculateRequirements back on for smaller projects.

examPitfalls.title: Weighting Leaf Requirements before the top level
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Expanding the whole tree immediately and assigning weights bottom-up.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Best practice is to weight top-down: collapse sub-Requirements, weight the highest level first to identify the risky area, then expand and weight the Leaf Requirements to pinpoint the exact item.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the correct structural order when building a Requirements tree in Tosca, from top to bottom?
practiceQuiz.hint: Folders organize the section; RequirementSets group Requirements by aspect or process view; Requirements can then be layered.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The structure is always Folder → RequirementSet → Requirement, with Requirements optionally containing sub-Requirements down to Leaf Requirements.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Requirement has a Frequency Class of 3 and a Damage Class of 2. Using the default base value of 2, how is its Complex Weight calculated?
practiceQuiz.hint: Complex Weighting is exponential, not additive — each class is raised to the power of the base value.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The formula is Weight = 2^(Frequency Class) × 2^(Damage Class), so 2^3 × 2^2 = 8 × 4 = 32. The exponential nature spreads Requirements apart more clearly than a simple sum would.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which statement correctly distinguishes Contribution (%) from Relative Weight (%) in the Requirements section?

options.text: Relative Weight (%) sums to 100% among siblings on the same level; Contribution (%) is parent-weighted and reflects share of the whole RequirementSet.
Both always sum to 100% across the entire RequirementSet.
Contribution (%) sums to 100% among siblings; Relative Weight (%) reflects the whole set.
They are two different names for the same calculated value.

practiceQuiz.hint: One column compares a Requirement only to its siblings; the other multiplies through parent weights.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Relative Weight (%) always sums to 100% for Requirements on the same level. Contribution (%) multiplies a Requirement's weight by its parents' weights, showing its true share of risk coverage across the entire RequirementSet.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A tester on Tosca 10.4 links a new TestCase to a Requirement but the Requirements section doesn't reflect the change. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

options.text: Requirements never update automatically in any Tosca version; a full project reload is required.
Since Tosca 10.3, auto-update is off by default; select the RequirementSet and press F6 (or click 'Update Outdated Values') to refresh, or enable AutoCalculateRequirements.
TestCases cannot be linked to Requirements at all.
The Weight formula needs to be recalculated manually every time.

practiceQuiz.hint: Look for the exclamation mark next to the RequirementSet — that's the tell.
practiceQuiz.rationale: From Tosca 10.3 onward, AutoCalculateRequirements defaults to off for performance in large repositories. An exclamation mark flags stale RequirementSets; F6 or 'Update Outdated Values' recalculates them, or the setting can be switched back on under Project >> Settings >> Commander >> General >> Advanced.

quickRecap.value: Folder → RequirementSet → Requirement → (optional) sub-Requirements, down to Leaf Requirements.
Single Weight column, 0-10 scale, best practice 1-5. Default weight is 1.
Weight = 2^(Frequency Class) × 2^(Damage Class) — exponential, base adjustable on the RequirementSet Properties tab.
Parent-weighted — a Requirement's true share of the whole RequirementSet.
Sibling-only comparison — always sums to 100% per level.
Always-on before 10.3; off by default from 10.3+ (toggle: AutoCalculateRequirements; manual refresh: F6 / Update Outdated Values).
